final.title: Keyboard Focus in Browser Games: WCAG 2.x Requirements and WCAG 3 Drafts
final.content:
For browser game developers, keyboard access is a core accessibility requirement. Published WCAG 2.x success criteria set the baseline for keyboard operability and visible focus. WCAG 3 materials are still drafts and should be treated as forward-looking, not final. This article focuses on practical keyboard focus checks for game menus, dialogs, settings, and non-pointer controls.

Key Points:
Success Criterion 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A) requires that all functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes, except where the underlying function requires input that depends on the path of the user's movement and not just the endpoints. For games, this means pointer-only actions such as drawing or freehand aiming may be exempt, but typical menu navigation, dialog choices, and non-path gameplay controls need keyboard equivalents.

SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible requires that any keyboard operable user interface has a mode of operation where the keyboard focus indicator is visible. In practice, use :focus-visible, avoid global outline removal, and check focus indicator contrast against adjacent colors.

The WCAG 3 support material on Focus user-controlled is explicitly a draft. It describes user-controlled and predictable focus as the default; automatic movement of focus after a user action is a limited exception, such as moving between fields for a time-based one-time password. It is not a published WCAG 2.x requirement.

Manual keyboard checks:
1. Disable pointer input or unplug the mouse.
2. Tab and Shift+Tab from initial focus through all keyboard-focusable interactive elements.
3. Confirm each keyboard-focusable interactive element receives a visible focus indicator.
4. Check that focus order matches the visual layout.
5. Activate every control using only the keyboard, including Enter/Space and arrow keys where expected.
6. Watch for focus loss, unexpected jumps, or controls that cannot be reached.
7. If focus moves automatically after a user action, verify that behavior against the WCAG 3 draft; document it separately from WCAG 2.x findings.

Run these checks early in development and after UI changes to catch focus regressions. Document any automatic focus movement as WCAG 3 draft behavior, not as a WCAG 2.x failure unless it causes a published criterion violation.

Analysis:
For browser games, ensure menus, buttons, dialog choices, settings, and non-pointer gameplay controls are reachable and operable with Tab/Shift+Tab, Enter/Space, arrow keys, or other keyboard equivalents. Pointer-only actions need a keyboard alternative unless the underlying function depends on movement path. The manual checks above are practical evidence-gathering techniques, not a guarantee of WCAG conformance. Use them with review of the applicable W3C Understanding documents: SC 2.1.1 (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/keyboard.html), SC 2.4.7 (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/focus-visible.html), and WCAG 3 draft Focus user-controlled (https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/informative/input-operation/keyboard-interface-input/focus-user-controlled/).

Conclusion:
Treat published WCAG 2.x criteria as the baseline for keyboard focus. Use the WCAG 3 drafts as optional, clearly labeled future direction. Early keyboard testing in browser games helps catch focus loss and unreachable controls before they become player-facing barriers.

output.title: Keyboard Focus in Browser Games: WCAG 2.x Requirements and Manual Checks
output.content:
For browser game developers, keyboard accessibility is often overlooked, but it is a baseline requirement under published WCAG 2.x guidance. Keyboard operability does not only help keyboard users; it also supports speech input, on-screen keyboards, and assistive technologies that send simulated keystrokes. For browser games, this is especially relevant because many games rely heavily on pointer input for menus and gameplay, but keyboard alternatives can widen the audience.

**Published WCAG 2.x criteria**

Success Criterion 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A) requires that all functionality be available through a keyboard interface, except where the underlying function requires freehand movement, such as drawing or freehand aiming (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/keyboard.html). Guideline 2.1 Keyboard Accessible states that this supports keyboard users, speech input, on-screen keyboards, and assistive technologies that produce simulated keystrokes (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/keyboard-accessible).

Success Criterion 2.4.7 Focus Visible requires every interactive element to have a visible focus indicator. Practical guidance from accessibility.build recommends using :focus-visible, never removing the outline, and checking contrast against adjacent colors (https://accessibility.build/wcag/2-4-7).

For browser games, this means menus, buttons, dialog choices, settings, and non-pointer gameplay controls should be reachable and operable with Tab/Shift+Tab, Enter/Space, arrow keys, or other keyboard equivalents. Pointer-only actions need a keyboard alternative unless the underlying function is a freehand movement.

**Draft WCAG 3 material**

Separately, the WCAG 3 support material on Focus user-controlled is explicitly marked as draft. It describes focus automatically moving to the next interactive element in keyboard navigation order after completion of a user action, such as moving between fields for a time-based one-time password code (https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/informative/input-operation/keyboard-interface-input/focus-user-controlled/). This is exploratory guidance, not a final WCAG requirement. Do not treat it as conformance criteria.

**Manual keyboard checks for games**

Use the following practical checks as evidence gathering. They do not guarantee WCAG conformance and should be combined with review of the applicable WCAG 2.x and draft WCAG 3 materials.

1. Unplug the mouse or disable pointer input.
2. Tab from the initial focus through all interactive elements.
3. Confirm each interactive element receives a visible focus indicator.
4. Confirm the focus order matches the visual layout.
5. Activate every control using only the keyboard.
6. Watch for focus loss, unexpected jumps, or controls that cannot be reached.
7. If focus moves automatically after a user action, verify that behavior aligns with the draft Focus user-controlled note.

**Conclusion**

Keyboard focus is a concrete, testable part of game accessibility. Follow the published WCAG 2.x criteria for compliance work, review the WCAG 3 draft for forward-looking guidance, and document your manual checks honestly. Documenting your testing scope is important: mark which checks come from published WCAG 2.x and which from draft WCAG 3 material. A keyboard-only playthrough is a way to uncover blockers. These steps help ensure your browser game is operable by a wider range of players.

issues.detail: SC 2.1.1 paraphrase omits the normative 'without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes' clause and broadens the exception to 'freehand movement' instead of path-dependent movement.
SC 2.4.7 is overstated as requiring every interactive element to have a visible focus indicator; the normative requirement applies to keyboard operable user interfaces.

The WCAG 3 'Focus user-controlled' draft is described as primarily about automatic focus movement, but it concerns user-controlled and predictable focus; automatic movement is a limited exception, not the central point.
SC 2.4.7 practical guidance cites accessibility.build rather than an official W3C resource. Secondary sources should be clearly labeled or supplemented with official guidance.
Manual check 3 says 'each interactive element,' which may overstate the scope; it should refer to keyboard-focusable interactive elements.

suggestions: Link directly to the normative WCAG 2.1 SC 2.1.1 text in addition to the Understanding document.
Use official W3C examples for the path-dependent exception, such as freehand drawing, rather than 'freehand aiming' unless explicitly sourced.
Clarify again in the conclusion that WCAG 3 is draft material and cannot create conformance obligations.
Consider referencing WCAG 2.2 Focus Appearance or Focus Not Obscured criteria where relevant for additional forward-looking guidance.

issues.detail: Focus order is checked but not explicitly tied to SC 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A). Consider linking it for completeness.
SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible level is omitted; it is Level AA in WCAG 2.1/2.2. Add level for consistency.
Focus indicator contrast against adjacent colors is a best practice not directly required by SC 2.4.7; clarify to avoid implying it is required at that SC.

suggestions: Add SC 2.4.3 Focus Order and SC 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap as baseline criteria for menu/dialog focus behavior.
Include guidance for canvas/WebGL game UIs: use DOM overlays, roving tabindex, or focusable elements with appropriate ARIA roles, and manage keyboard focus manually.
Consider using WCAG 2.2 references instead of only WCAG 2.1 Understanding links.
Add a note that contrast of focus indicator may be required by WCAG 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (AAA) or 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast if claiming that level.

output.projectName: Game Accessibility Guidelines: WCAG Keyboard Focus
output.goal: Provide practical, evidence-based keyboard focus guidance for browser game developers, citing W3C sources, distinguishing published WCAG 2.x from WCAG 3 drafts, and offering manual keyboard checks without claiming compliance.

phases.name: Scope and source review
tasks: Review published WCAG 2.1/2.2 keyboard-related success criteria: 2.1.1 Keyboard, 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap, 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts, 2.4.3 Focus Order, 2.4.7 Focus Visible, 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (2.2).
Cite W3C URLs: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/ and https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/.
Review WCAG 3 draft at https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/ as informative only; mark as draft and not for compliance claims.
Define scope for browser game contexts: menus, HUD, dialogs, game canvas alternatives.

phases.name: Draft keyboard focus guidance
tasks: Write guidance for keyboard-only play: all game controls reachable and operable via keyboard; no keyboard trap.
Address focus visible requirements: minimum contrast/area for focus indicator; avoid off-screen or clipped focus.
Address focus order: logical DOM order matches visual game flow; dynamic UI updates maintain focus.
Include manual checks: Tab/Shift+Tab through menus; Enter/Space activate; arrow keys navigate; Esc closes dialogs without trapping focus.
Include WCAG 2.1.4 character key shortcuts guidance: allow remap/disable single-key shortcuts unless necessary.

phases.name: Developer implementation notes
tasks: Provide code-level examples for focus management in HTML5 canvas/WebGL games (e.g., tabindex, roving tabindex, aria-activedescendant).
Recommend testing with real keyboards and screen readers (NVDA/JAWS) for browser games.
Distinguish WCAG 2.x normative vs WCAG 3 outcomes/assertions; cite draft URL.
Add warning: following this plan does not guarantee WCAG compliance; seek formal audit.

phases.name: Manual QA and validation
tasks: Execute manual keyboard-only test script on 3 browser games.
Check focus visibility, focus order, keyboard trap, character key shortcuts.
Document failures with screenshots and W3C SC references.
Collect source URLs for each finding.

phases.name: Final review and publication
tasks: Cross-check all guidance against WCAG 2.1/2.2 and WCAG 3 draft citations.
Remove any compliance guarantee language.
Add disclaimer: WCAG 3 is not final; public draft may change.
Publish as internal guidance for browser game team.

risks: WCAG 3 draft content may change before final publication, making citations obsolete.
Game developers may rely on the guide as legal compliance without a formal audit.
Browser game canvas focus management may require ARIA patterns beyond the scope of this guide.
Manual keyboard testing may miss complex game interactions not covered by WCAG keyboard success criteria.

Use them with review of the applicable W3C Understanding documents: SC 2.1.1 (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/keyboard.html), SC 2.4.7 (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/focus-visible.html), and WCAG 3 draft Focus user-controlled (https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/informative/input-operation/keyboard-interface-input/focus-user-controlled/).

Conclusion:
Treat published WCAG 2.x criteria as the baseline for keyboard focus. Use the WCAG 3 drafts as optional, clearly labeled future direction. Early keyboard testing in browser games helps catch focus loss and unreachable controls before they become player-facing barriers.
content.style: Practical evidence-based guidance; cite source URLs; distinguish published WCAG 2.x from WCAG 3 drafts. Provide manual keyboard checks. Do not claim these notes guarantee compliance.
appliedRevisionNotes: Revise the SC 2.1.1 description to include 'without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes' and replace 'freehand movement' with the WCAG exception for input that depends on the path of movement and not just endpoints.
Correct the SC 2.4.7 statement to match the normative wording: any keyboard operable user interface has a mode of operation where the keyboard focus indicator is visible.
Rewrite the WCAG 3 'Focus user-controlled' description to accurately reflect that it is about user-controlled and predictable focus, with automatic movement only as a limited exception.
Adjust manual check 3 and related language to refer to keyboard-focusable interactive elements rather than all interactive elements.
Supplement or replace the accessibility.build citation with the official W3C/WCAG Understanding SC 2.4.7 resource.
